lesson.title: Concave Up: When the Graph Holds Water
lesson.summary: A function is concave up on exactly the intervals where f'' is positive, meaning its slope is continually increasing there, and every tangent line drawn on such an interval sits below the curve.
lesson.body:
An interval where f''(x) is greater than 0 for every x in it is called an interval of concavity up, or simply concave up. On such an interval, f' is an increasing function in its own right, so every tangent line drawn to the graph on that interval sits below the curve, touching at one point and then falling away underneath as x moves away from the point of tangency in either direction. That is the geometric signature of a graph shaped like the inside of a bowl.

For the cubic f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5, the concave up interval was found to be (1, positive infinity) using f''(x) = 6(x - 1). A quick second check at x = 5 confirms it: f''(5) = 6(5 - 1) = 24, positive, consistent with the earlier test at x = 2. Some functions are concave up across their entire domain rather than just a piece of it. For f(x) = x^2, f''(x) = 2, a positive constant, so the familiar parabola is concave up everywhere, which matches its bowl-like graph. For f(x) = e^x, f''(x) = e^x, which is positive for every real x, so the exponential curve is concave up along its entire length as well, bending upward more and more sharply as x grows.

Recognizing a concave up stretch matters beyond just describing the shape of a graph. Wherever a function is concave up, any tangent line drawn there gives an underestimate of the function's true values nearby, since the curve pulls away above the tangent. That fact is used constantly in error estimates, and it is also the geometric reason a critical point sitting inside a concave up region, where f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) is greater than 0, must be a local minimum, exactly the logic behind the Second Derivative Test.
